source: Kapur (2006) Productive failure: a hidden efficacy of seemingly unproductive production (ICLS paper; precursor of Kapur 2008)
finding: First test of the idea. Groups that worked on ill-structured physics problems with no scaffolds did badly as groups, yet later beat scaffolded groups on individual well-structured and ill-structured post-tests.
numbers: N=309 11th-grade science students, 7 Indian schools, 103 triads randomly assigned: 50 ill-structured (IS) groups vs 53 well-structured (WS) groups. Two 1.5 h group problems in text chat, then individual post-tests. HLM: IS beat WS on the well-structured post-test (chi2=22.82, p<.001) and on the ill-structured post-test (chi2=27.21, p<.001). WS groups had higher convergence (F=10.01, p=.002, partial eta2=.09).
quote: despite failing in their problem-solving efforts, these participants outperformed their counterparts in the wellstructured condition on transfer measures
limits: Group chat with high-school students on kinematics; the contrasting-case step (ill then well-structured problems) is part of the treatment, so it is not a clean test of order alone. No delayed test. Single-author, no independent replication of this exact design found.
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim that a failed first attempt can carry value. Suggests the first attempt should be allowed to stay unaided, but the value was extracted later by contrast with a structured problem, so the lesson step matters.

source: Kapur (2006) ICLS paper: process data and theory
finding: Process coding showed why the unscaffolded groups looked like they failed: more problem analysis, critique and criteria talk, less solution development; divergent, less convergent talk. Kapur explains the later gain with complexity theory (edge of chaos) and argues for innovation over efficiency, departing from the balanced optimal adaptability corridor of Schwartz et al. (2005).
numbers: IS groups: more problem analysis (F=18.20, partial eta2=.16), problem critique (F=11.91, eta2=.11), criteria development (F=4.09, eta2=.04). WS groups: more solution development (F=7.23, eta2=.07) and solution evaluation (F=10.66, eta2=.10). Lag-sequential: IS groups at least twice as likely to show PA-PC, PA-CD, CD-SD transitions and feedback loops SE-PA, SE-PC.
quote: over time as sufficient complexity builds up in a system, there comes a critical point where order emerges spontaneously and for free
limits: The complexity-theory account is a metaphor, not a tested model. Coding of chat by two raters (Krippendorff alpha .84).
agent_relevance: Gives the earliest mechanism claim: wide, divergent exploration builds problem structure that later instruction can use. Maps loosely to letting the agent produce several different attempts before it is shown the canonical method.

source: Kapur (2009) Designing for productive failure in mathematical problem solving (CogSci), Study 1 (School A)
finding: 7th graders in Singapore on average speed. Productive failure (PF) class solved ill-structured problems in groups with no help, mostly failed, then got a teacher consolidation. They beat a lecture-and-practice (LP) class on both well-structured and complex post-test items, even though LP got homework and feedback.
numbers: 75 students, 2 intact classes (PF n=37, LP n=38); pretest no difference F(1,73)=.177, p=.675. Only 11% and 21% of groups solved the two group problems (avg 16%); individual extension problems solved by 3% and 20% (avg 11.5%); mean confidence 1.22/4. Post-test MANOVA F(2,71)=5.64, p=.005, partial eta2=.144. Well-structured items (max 32): PF 30.61 (SD 4.09) vs LP 28.89 (SD 4.26), F(1,72)=4.78, p=.032, eta2=.06. Complex item (max 7): PF 4.35 (SD 2.13) vs LP 2.77 (SD 2.12), F(1,72)=10.11, p=.002, eta2=.12.
limits: Intact classes, quasi-experiment, one teacher, no random assignment, immediate post-test. The PF students did not practise the method.
agent_relevance: Core effect size pattern: failure rate during the attempt is high (about 84% to 89% fail) yet later conceptual and transfer scores rise. A low success rate on first attempt is by design, not a defect to fix.

source: Kapur (2009) CogSci paper, Study 2 (School B, lower ability)
finding: Replicated Study 1 in a school with much lower mathematical ability. Both PF classes (two teachers) beat the LP class on well-structured and complex items; no difference on the tabular item (the representation LP had practised) and on the graphical item.
numbers: 114 students in 3 intact classes (PF-A n=38, PF-B n=36, LP n=40). Well-structured (max 19): PF-B 16.30, PF-A 15.30, LP 14.30, F(2,110)=5.26, p=.007, partial eta2=.09. Complex item (max 7): PF-B 3.86, PF-A 2.58, LP 1.01, F(2,110)=17.98, p<.001, eta2=.25. Tabular item (max 6): LP 3.30, PF-B 2.80, PF-A 2.34, F(2,110)=1.09, p=.339. Graphical item (max 3): 1.97/1.95/1.70, p=.133. Overall MANOVA F(8,212)=6.48, p<.001, eta2=.20.
limits: Intact classes again; same research group; PF teacher identity partly confounded with class.
agent_relevance: Boundary note: the largest gain is on the complex, transfer-type item, and LP is not worse on the drilled item. Suggests the lessons stored after a failed attempt should target concept structure, not only the procedure.

source: Kapur (2011) Designing for productive failure (J. Learning Sciences) with Kapur and Bielaczyc 2012 design principles
finding: Three Singapore schools, average to low ability 7th graders. PF students produced many linked representations and methods but did not solve the problems, then beat direct-instruction students on well-structured and complex post-test problems, and showed more representational flexibility on graphs that were not taught.
numbers: Abstract only (OpenAlex text): 3 studies, PF vs DI; effect numbers not read this session.
limits: Abstract-level record only.
agent_relevance: Confirms the paradigm spans ability levels. Representational flexibility is the part most similar to an agent holding several solution forms.

source: Kapur and Rummel (2012) Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities (Instructional Science editorial)
finding: Defines the design: a generation phase (students produce several representations and solution methods, RSMs, for a novel complex problem) followed by a consolidation phase (compare, contrast, organise student RSMs into the canonical one). Separates productive success from productive failure. Roots: desirable difficulties (Schmidt and Bjork 1992), preparation for future learning (Schwartz and Bransford 1998), inventing (Schwartz and Martin 2004).
numbers: Editorial for four studies from Singapore, Germany, Canada, USA. Kapur: 9th graders, variance; PF students produced diverse formulations, failed to reach the canonical one, DI students did better on practice but PF beat DI on conceptual understanding and transfer without losing procedural fluency; diversity of RSMs correlated with learning.
quote: Designing for productive failure involves two phases: a generation (or invention) phase followed by a consolidation (or instruction) phase.
limits: Editorial summary of other papers; no new data.
agent_relevance: The cleanest statement of the two-phase protocol. Our schema analogue: attempt phase producing several candidates, then a consolidation step that compares them to the canonical method before storing the lesson.

source: Westermann and Rummel (2012) Delaying instruction: evidence from a study in a university relearning setting (as summarised in Kapur and Rummel 2012)
finding: Supporting the generation phase with a role script (Think Ask Understand) in a relearning setting at university. Script groups beat direct instruction in all weeks except the first, so the gain grew as students got used to the script.
numbers: 76 university (Masters) students, 4-week in vivo experiment, 4 topics of mathematical analysis; TAU > DI in weeks 2 to 4 (test statistics not given in the editorial).
limits: Read via the editorial summary, not the primary paper. Support during generation is not the pure Kapur design.
agent_relevance: Suggests that unaided first attempts may need a minimal procedural frame the first time; benefit built up over repeated rounds. Relevant to carrying lessons across tasks.

source: Roll et al. (2012) and Wiedmann et al. (2012) in Kapur and Rummel (2012): support during invention
finding: Metacognitive prompts (questions, self-explanation, peer interaction) during invention improved the conceptual quality of invented methods and strategy use, but not the mathematical quality of expressions. Group composition mattered: groups need at least one high-ability member; mixed groups generated the widest range of RSMs and used the later canonical formula better.
numbers: Roll: first-year physics lab, slope uncertainty; guided invention (GI) vs unguided (UI); GI invented methods with more conceptual features and ranked datasets more accurately. Wiedmann: two studies with undergraduates on variance; effect sizes not given in editorial.
limits: Second-hand summary of two papers.
agent_relevance: Both point to diversity of attempts as the driver. For one agent, diversity must come from the program (varied prompts or constraints), not from persona voters (see G4).

source: Kapur (2014) Comparing learning from productive failure and vicarious failure (J. Learning Sciences)
finding: Students who generated their own failed solutions learned more than students who only evaluated other students' failed solutions, when both then got the same instruction. Self-generated failure beat vicarious failure on conceptual understanding and transfer, not on procedural fluency.
numbers: Abstract only: 136 eighth-grade students, 2 Singapore schools, concept of variance. PF reported greater mental effort and interest in the canonical solution than VF; no difference in engagement. Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Later replication in Germany (Brand et al. 2024, 110 students) found overlapping processes in PF and VF and learner-specific effects.
agent_relevance: Key for an agent: failed attempts the agent itself produced may teach more than failed attempts imported from elsewhere. Argues against filling the lesson memory with other agents' failures only.

source: Kapur (2016) Examining productive failure, productive success, unproductive failure, and unproductive success in learning (Educational Psychologist)
finding: Theory paper. Crosses initial performance (success or failure) with later learning (productive or unproductive) to give four designs. Argues direct instruction can be an unproductive success and that a large design space lies between discovery and direct instruction.
numbers: No new data in the abstract; 630 citations (OpenAlex).
limits: Abstract only. A framework, not a computational model.
agent_relevance: Gives the 4-way vocabulary for logging agent runs: the cell that matters is failed first attempt followed by improved later transfer. Passing the first attempt is not evidence of learning.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure (Review of Educational Research), meta-analysis
finding: Problem solving then instruction (PS-I) beats instruction then problem solving (I-PS) on average, more so with high fidelity to PF principles. Older learners and longer interventions gain more. Younger learners (grades 2 to 5) and domain-general skills favoured I-PS.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Overall Hedges g=0.36 [95% CI 0.20, 0.51]. High-fidelity PF: g from 0.37 to 0.58. Bias-adjusted true effect g=0.87 (authors' own estimate).
limits: Abstract only (full text blocked, HTTP 403). Authors are the PF originator; the bias-adjusted g of 0.87 is much larger than the raw estimate and is a model-based correction, which should be read with caution. Quasi-experiments inflate the effect.
agent_relevance: The one number to carry: about 0.36 standard deviations on average, larger when fidelity is high. Expect a modest gain, not a large one, and not for domain-general skills.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021, EdArXiv) From problem-solving to sensemaking: a comparative meta-analysis of preparatory approaches for future learning
finding: Adding scaffolds to the problem-solving phase did not help over unscaffolded problem solving. Problem-solving first had a non-significant moderate edge over a sensemaking preparatory activity.
numbers: 33 articles, 118 comparisons. PS-I vs scaffolded PS-I: g=-0.08 [-0.20, 0.04]; Bayesian probability the difference is below 0.2 is 99%. PS-I vs sensemaking: g=0.22 [-0.06, 0.51]; 40.37% chance of at least a moderate advantage. Bias-corrected: g=0.55 and 0.64.
limits: Preprint, read from a repository summary page (fetch tool summary), not the PDF. Bias-correction estimates are model-dependent.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding the first attempt buys nothing on average, so a cheap unaided first attempt is enough; no extra hint machinery is needed before the lesson.

source: Glogger-Frey, Fleischer, Gruny, Kappich, Renkl (2015, ICLS version 2013) Inventing prepares learning motivationally, but a worked-out solution enhances learning outcomes
finding: A counter-result. Inventing criteria made pre-service teachers feel more knowledge gaps, curiosity and interest, but a worked-out solution gave better learning.
numbers: N=44 (42 in main analyses), student teachers learning criteria to evaluate learning strategies. Solution group beat inventing group: F(1,38)=4.95, p=.032, d=-0.72 with prior knowledge controlled. Invention group worked from M=2.8 (SD 1.31) appropriate invented solutions; their appropriateness correlated with outcome r=.52, p=.028. Learning time was the only mediator (r=.55).
limits: Small sample, one domain; the worked solution was an optimal, given solution to the same problem.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: when the first attempt is poor, showing a worked solution may do better. A scaffold that lets the agent compare its attempt to a correct one may beat a lesson from failure alone.

source: Glogger-Frey et al. (2022) How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affects subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers (Instructional Science)
finding: Replicated the 2013 result with think-aloud: worked-example group outperformed inventing group on transfer, and showed more elaboration and more use of the canonical solution in the later phase.
numbers: Abstract only: N=45; transfer difference with Bayes factor BF+0 > 313; learning-process differences with BFs around 4. No motivational difference this time.
limits: Abstract only. Pre-service teachers, one domain.
agent_relevance: Second report that a given correct solution can beat an open invention task. Weighs against making failure a rule.

source: Chowrira, Smith, Dubois and Roll (2019) DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course (npj Science of Learning)
finding: PF designed and taught by ordinary course instructors, not learning scientists, in a big first-year biology class. PF section scored about 5 points higher on the topic items of the next midterm; the effect was largest for weaker students and mostly gone on the final.
numbers: Quasi-experiment: PF section 295 students vs active-learning section 279. Midterm 2 topics: b=4.78 percentage points, 95% CI [2.19, 7.36], effect size 0.32 [0.15, 0.49], R2=0.43. Final exam: b=0.78, CI [-2.80, 4.36], p=.668. By prior-ability tercile on Midterm 2: Low b=8.28 (p<.001), Med b=3.26 (p=.193), High b=3.37 (p=.105); Med+High combined b=3.25 (p=.045). Low group still ahead on the final (about 7 points, marginal).
limits: Sections not randomised. The PF section already had higher grades (about 16 points in general advantage, d=0.42; Midterm 1 gap d=0.44), so the covariates carry the weight. The comparison is against active learning, not lecture.
agent_relevance: Real-class evidence of a small, decaying effect with benefit concentrated in weak performers. If our agent is already strong on a task type, expect less gain from a failure-first step.

source: Nachtigall, Serova and Rummel (2020) When failure fails to be productive (Instructional Science), Study 1
finding: Failed replication outside STEM. 10th graders learning principles of experimental design in social science research methods. PF students did worse than direct-instruction (DI) students on application and transfer items and on the whole post-test.
numbers: N=212 (quasi-experiment, 11 clusters). Transfer scale F(1,210)=31.11, p<.001, partial eta2=.13, in favour of DI. Total outcome F(1,209)=27.46, p<.001, eta2=.12, DI better. Only 24% of PF students vs 48% of DI students solved a familiar post-test task canonically.
quote: PF students did not outperform DI students on learning social science research methods.
limits: Quasi-experiment, classes as clusters. Authors suggest perceived competence of PF students was higher than DI students after the first phase and fell (study 1), contrary to PF theory.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that failure-first can hurt in a non-STEM, less-formal domain. Domain gate needed: apply failure-first only where the target is a compact structured concept.

source: Nachtigall, Serova and Rummel (2020), Study 2
finding: Second study with 11th graders (evaluating research designs) found no PF effect either way. Design fidelity was checked: students generated solution ideas and showed knowledge-activation and knowledge-gap awareness, yet learning did not improve.
numbers: N=152 (PF n=80, DI n=72). Transfer scale F(1,149)=0.09, p=.77, partial eta2=.001. Total learning outcome F(1,148)=0.32, p=.57, partial eta2=.002. Only 9% of PF vs 18% of DI students solved a familiar task canonically.
limits: Null result with covariate adjustment; 7 clusters. Not a proof of absence in other non-STEM domains.
agent_relevance: Even when mechanism checks pass (prior knowledge activated, gaps noticed), the benefit can be absent. Do not treat activation of prior knowledge as proof the lesson will be useful.

source: Loibl and Leuders (2024) Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication (Instructional Science 53)
finding: Failed conceptual replication of Loibl and Rummel (2014) with Bayesian reasoning. No main effect of problem-solving-first vs instruction-first, and no effect of building the instruction on typical student solutions. Authors explain: students only activated prior probability knowledge and did not explore the solution space or notice their gaps; the typical solutions in the instruction did not match what students had produced.
numbers: 75 students in a 2x2 design (PS-I vs I-PS; instruction with or without typical student solutions). Order of phases: no significant difference (F(1,71)=0.06 reported for order on one measure); typical-solutions factor on another hypothesis F(1,71)=0.04, p=.84. Exact mapping of each F to each measure was not checked.
limits: Small sample; one domain. The original effects were on variance, which is a better fit for invention tasks.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: PF needs an open solution space the learner can actually explore, and the consolidation must match the attempts the learner made. For an agent, a lesson should be tied to the agent's own failed outputs, not generic ones.

source: Loibl and Leukel (2023) and the follow-up on javelin throwing in primary school (Instructional Science 2025)
finding: Problem-solving before instruction helped secondary pupils learning a motor skill (Loibl and Leukel 2023) but did not help 4th graders. Both orders improved movement features; neither improved throwing distance.
numbers: Abstract only: 50 fourth graders across I-PS, PS-I and PS-I with extra practice; no significant order effect; no significant gain in distance.
limits: Abstract only. Authors point to young children's weak ability to build declarative knowledge during problem solving.
agent_relevance: Age and prior declarative knowledge matter: the learner needs enough base knowledge to link the attempt to the lesson. An agent with a weak base on a topic may gain less.

source: Suriyaarachchi, Denny and Nanayakkara (2025) Investigating the use of productive failure as a design paradigm for learning introductory Python programming (SIGCSE TS 2025)
finding: Programming domain. Students who tackled a list problem first (PF) failed more on that first task but did better two weeks later on a similar task, and showed a larger drop in cognitive load (heart-rate variability).
numbers: 20 recruited, 16 analysed (DI n=9, PF n=7). Weather-station task success: DI 8/9, PF 2/7. Heart-rate task same session: DI 8/9, PF 7/7. Same task after two weeks: DI 6/9, PF 7/7. 9 of 16 students preferred PF.
limits: Tiny sample, no significance tests in the success table, individual sessions, wearable-sensor proxy for load. Not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Shows the PF signature in code: low first-attempt success, equal-or-better delayed reuse. Closest human result to a coding agent keeping lessons from a failed first program.

source: Puech, Macina, Chatain, Sachan and Kapur (2025) Towards the pedagogical steering of large language models for tutoring: a case study with modeling productive failure (Findings of ACL; arXiv 2410.03781)
finding: Builds StratL, an algorithm that makes an LLM follow a multi-turn PF tutoring plan: a student-state tracer labels each reply, a hand-built transition graph picks the next tutoring intent, and the intent is added to the prompt. The LLM does not choose the next step; code does. A prompted LLM that chose intents itself was worse than the coded graph.
numbers: Simulated students (3 conversations x 2 problems per version). Mean student-generated RSMs: StratL 2.34, no-intent baseline 1.00, constant intent 1.34, LLM-chosen intent 1.34. PF score on Consistency problem (max 4): StratL 3.67, baseline 1.33, constant 4.00, LLM-intent 3.67; on Country problem: 4.00, 0.44, 4.00, 3.11. State tracer micro F1 = 0.77.
limits: Fidelity to PF process, not learning gains, is what was measured. Simulated students are LLMs. Rubric scored by the authors.
agent_relevance: Directly matches our design rule that code decides transitions and the model fills slots (Section 1 of the schema). Shows a plain LLM leaks the answer; a coded plan holds the PF order.

source: Puech et al. (2025), field study with students
finding: With real 9th graders, the steered tutor produced the PF behaviour (more solution attempts, fewer hints) but students found it less helpful.
numbers: 17 Singapore 9th graders, 15 minutes each, random assignment to StratL (V1) or the baseline (V2), two exercises. PF score higher for V1 (p=.046, 2-sample t-test, Consistency problem); student-generated RSMs 2.6 on average for V1 vs about 1 for V2 (p=.05). Helpfulness (3-point): V1 1.20 vs V2 2.00 on Consistency; 2.67 vs 2.80 on Country. Coherence and empathy not significantly different.
limits: Very small N, p-values at the edge, no learning measure or delayed test. Student State Tracing errors made the tutor contradict itself once (a student complained it kept asking to check a correct answer).
agent_relevance: Result for design: withholding the answer raises the number of attempts but lowers felt helpfulness, so the agent should use code-set limits for how long to withhold. No measured learning benefit from an LLM-run PF exists in this paper.

source: Rotter, Benazet i Montobbio and Hernandez-Leo (2026, arXiv 2605.15850) Access timing as scaffolding: a reinforcement learning approach to GenAI in education
finding: An RL agent decides when students may use GenAI, with a reward built partly on productive failure (reward for access after struggle). Timed access beat unrestricted access on the post-test and matched full withholding.
numbers: N=105 higher-education students (Always n=36, RL n=37, Never n=32). Post-test (0 to 8): Always 4.03 (SD 1.83), RL 5.11 (SD 1.85), Never 5.25 (SD 2.00). RL vs Always t(71)=2.51, p=.014, d=0.59. RL vs Never t(67)=-0.30, p=.762, d=-0.07. Mean AI requests: Always 11.25, RL 2.46, Never 0. No condition effect on metacognitive gain (all p above .4).
limits: Preprint. The test is of timing as a whole, not PF alone; timed access did not beat no access. Lab study, short, one task.
agent_relevance: Human-AI result: unrestricted answer access hurts; delayed access is no worse than none. Supports a rule where the agent must attempt before it may consult retrieved solutions or memory.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS)
finding: Large randomised field trial. A plain GPT-4 helper raised practice scores but lowered later unassisted exam scores. A GPT-4 tutor with hints, teacher-written solutions, and no direct answers removed the harm. Students in the plain arm did not notice they had learned less.
numbers: About 1,000 students in about 50 classes of grades 9 to 11 at one Turkish school, four 90-minute sessions, pre-registered, randomised by class. Practice score: +0.137 (GPT Base) and +0.361 (GPT Tutor) out of 1, i.e. +48% and +127% over control. Exam without AI: GPT Base -0.054 (-17%), GPT Tutor -0.004 (not different from control). GPT-4 gave wrong answers on the practice problems at a measurable logical and arithmetic error rate. In GPT Base, common student messages were repeat the question (38%) and ask for answers (29%).
limits: One school, one subject, short horizon. GPT Tutor prompt was far longer than GPT Base's, so guardrail design and prompt effort are bundled. Not a PF test, though it shows the same performance-vs-learning gap.
agent_relevance: The best LLM-era proof of Kapur's performance-learning gap in people. For our agent the lesson is on the other side: an agent that is handed answers looks better on the task while retaining nothing.

source: Akgun and Toker (2025, arXiv 2504.10249) Struggle first, prompt later: how task complexity shapes learning with GenAI-assisted pretesting
finding: Students who attempted a problem before they were allowed to ask ChatGPT scored higher on the final test than those who used ChatGPT at once (Study 1). Making the pre-attempt adaptive (AI-generated questions) did not raise scores over fixed questions (Study 2). Study 3 with a more complex exploratory task showed a moderate gain.
numbers: Study 1: 60 students analysed (31 no-pretest, 29 pretest), final test no-pretest M=78.59 (SD 7.62) vs pretest M=91.85 (SD 9.52), t(58)=5.979, p<.001, d=1.543; prior recall equal (71.03 vs 72.90). Study 2 (n=78): fixed vs adaptive, t(76)=1.002, p=.319. Study 3 (n=87): final test F(1,85)=5.839, p=.018, partial eta2=.064.
limits: Preprint, a pretest-then-LLM design (not full PF with consolidation), small samples, effect size in Study 1 is very large and from one session. Authors did not report a delayed test in what was read.
agent_relevance: Shows an attempt-before-consult rule helps people use an LLM well. For the agent, an equivalent is to write its own attempt before reading stored lessons or tools.

source: Lehmann, Cornelius and Sting (2025, arXiv 2409.09047) AI meets the classroom: when do large language models harm learning?
finding: In two pre-registered lab experiments the LLM had no average effect on learning. Usage mattered: asking an LLM to produce solutions to exercises (substituting for work) raised the volume of topics covered and lowered understanding of each, while asking for explanations (complementing) raised understanding. The LLM widened the gap between low and high prior-knowledge students.
numbers: Python learning, mostly novices (79% to 78% no prior experience). In Study 3, 42% of messages asking for a solution were sent without a single attempt by the student. Effect tables not read in detail this session.
limits: Exploratory split by behaviour (self-selected), not randomised; numbers for the usage effects not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Same direction as the PF rule: attempt first, ask second. Also hints that strong agents benefit most from lessons while weak ones need support.

source: Brand et al. (2024) Investigating learner characteristics and processes in productive failure and vicarious failure to design adaptive guidance (Learning and Instruction 102052)
finding: Mathematics students in PF (own attempts) and VF (studying others' attempts) showed largely the same learning processes; VF learners were more analytical, PF learners more solution-oriented. Ability, prior knowledge and self-concept moderated what helped.
numbers: Abstract only: 110 secondary school students; think-aloud from 15 PF-VF pairs.
limits: Abstract only. Small process sample.
agent_relevance: Suggests the failure-first step is not uniform: its value depends on the learner's starting knowledge and confidence. Gate failure-first by estimated competence of the agent on that task type.

source: Loibl, Roll and Rummel (2017) Towards a theory of when and how problem solving followed by instruction supports learning (Educational Psychology Review), as cited in Nachtigall et al. (2020) and Loibl and Leuders (2024)
finding: Names three mechanisms behind the PS-I benefit: activation of prior knowledge, awareness of knowledge gaps, and recognition of deep features in the later instruction. Names design features that trigger them: an open task with rich solution space, and instruction that compares student solutions to the canonical one.
numbers: No data; theory. Mechanism list was read in Nachtigall et al. (2020), not in the original paper (full text not fetched).
limits: Secondhand through two replication papers. Mechanism tests in Nachtigall found prior-knowledge activation and gap awareness present but no learning gain, so the mechanisms are necessary at best, not sufficient.
agent_relevance: The nearest thing to a formal model of PF. Maps to three agent signals that code can log: which prior method was tried, which check failed (gap), and which feature of the lesson separates the right method from the wrong ones.

source: Schwartz and Martin (2004) Inventing to prepare for future learning: the hidden efficiency of encouraging original student production in statistics instruction (Cognition and Instruction 22)
finding: Ninth graders who first invented a formula (reliability of a measure) and then heard a lecture matched tell-and-practice students on standard transfer and beat them only when the test included a learning resource. Replicated with classroom teachers in Study 2.
numbers: Percent-correct figures not retrieved; only the design and the pattern 'no difference without a learning resource, advantage with one' were seen in a search snippet.
limits: Search snippet only, full text not opened. Exact numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: The key moderator: the benefit appears when the test lets the learner learn something new, not on a closed-book test of the drilled procedure. A failed-first agent should be judged on how it handles new variants.
